item.text: {"facts":[{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":4,"end_unit":4,"fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19 reports persistent state and structural barriers to information access for Indigenous and rural communities, including inadequate culturally appropriate information, weak coordination, digital exclusion, and insufficient disaster-prevention policy; it states these problems persisted during López Obrador's administration.","question_ids":["3B.7","3B.9","4B.3","4B.6","4B.7","4B.10","6B.2","6B.3","6B.5","6B.8","6B.10","8B.6","8B.7","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Evidence concerns 2022 and is relevant to the inherited institutional posture entering 2023; the source was published in 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The report explicitly evaluates the federal government and programs under Andrés Manuel López Obrador, while some failures involve state and municipal authorities.","limitations":["The source is an advocacy organization's annual report and includes participant testimony, official data, and prior research.","It does not establish that every reported local failure was personally directed by López Obrador."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":5,"end_unit":6,"fact_summary":"In 2022 ARTICLE 19 documented 696 attacks against the press, including 12 journalist killings; 296 attacks were attributed directly to state actors, and 97% of press-violence cases remained impune. It also reports 176 stigmatizing comments in presidential-conference discourse, 44 of which were attacks on the press, including 33 directly by the president.","question_ids":["3B.3","3B.6","3B.8","3B.10","4B.3","4B.6","4B.9","4B.10","7B.1","7B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Direct evidence is for 2022, immediately preceding the target year and used to characterize the 2023 starting posture.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes 33 monitored attacks directly to López Obrador and separately reports broader state-actor participation in attacks.","limitations":["The attack totals cover Mexico and include actors beyond the federal executive.","ARTICLE 19's protocol distinguishes documented attacks from non-aggressive disagreement, but attribution of all attacks is not identical to presidential responsibility."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":7,"end_unit":7,"fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19 reports documented Pegasus espionage against human-rights defenders and journalists during the administration, including military surveillance, and states that the president denied the revelations while official resources were used to contest them; it also reports no effective accountability for the military's digital-security and surveillance failures.","question_ids":["1B.3","1B.7","1B.9","3B.2","3B.4","3B.5","3B.8","4B.3","4B.6","4B.9","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","7B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The cited espionage revelations and governmental response occurred in 2022 and bear directly on the posture entering 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes the denial and official counter-campaign to López Obrador and the surveillance to military institutions under federal authority.","limitations":["The source reports investigative findings and its own assessment; individual criminal responsibility is not finally adjudicated in these units.","The underlying Pegasus use began in earlier years, although the report describes continued use during the current administration."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":8,"end_unit":9,"fact_summary":"The report describes weak victim institutions: civil security and justice institutions received substantially less funding than military institutions; only 186 of 1,504 registered Mexico City victims received financial support; FEADLE had opened 1,592 investigations since 2010 but obtained only 32 sentences; and the protection mechanism had recurring risk-assessment, implementation, and coordination failures. It also notes a 46% budget increase and additional staffing for the protection mechanism as a partial positive development.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.6","3B.7","3B.9","3B.10","4B.4","4B.5","4B.10","6B.1","6B.2","6B.4","6B.5","6B.9","6B.10","8B.2","8B.3","8B.5","8B.6","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"Evidence concerns 2022 and early 2023 conditions, including the 2023 protection-mechanism budget.","ruler_attribution":"The report evaluates federal institutions and budgets under López Obrador, while some victim-service failures are specifically Mexico City or state-level.","limitations":["Budget increases are inputs and do not demonstrate effective outcomes.","The sentence count and impunity calculation do not by themselves establish the reasons for every unresolved case."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":10,"end_unit":10,"fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19 reports that the federal government emphasized symbolic and fragmented reparations, extended the Army's domestic deployment to 2028, transferred the National Guard to Sedena, recognized a large disappearance and forensic crisis, and was accused of attributing present failures to prior administrations while not fully assuming current responsibility.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.5","3B.6","3B.9","3B.10","4B.4","4B.10","7B.2","7B.7","7B.10","8B.2","8B.6","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The cited decisions and assessments concern 2022 and define the institutional context entering 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes the extension of military deployment and National Guard transfer to federal executive and legislative decisions under López Obrador.","limitations":["The report's causal and evaluative conclusions are those of ARTICLE 19 and affected communities.","The unit does not provide a complete account of all federal victim-support initiatives."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":12,"end_unit":14,"fact_summary":"Sembrando Vida and Benito Juárez scholarships provided substantial social transfers and reached millions, but documented beneficiaries faced opaque selection, inadequate information and training, reliance on WhatsApp despite digital exclusion, weak monitoring, payment irregularities, and burdensome travel; Coneval identified undefined targeting and program-goal indicators, while ASF-related reporting identified unexplained scholarship payments.","question_ids":["5B.1","5B.6","5B.7","5B.8","5B.10","6B.1","6B.2","6B.3","6B.4","6B.5","6B.7","6B.8","6B.10","8B.2","8B.3","8B.5","8B.6","8B.7","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"Program performance evidence is primarily 2021-2022, with 2023 operating rules cited; it informs the target-year starting conditions.","ruler_attribution":"The programs were presidential priorities operated by federal agencies under López Obrador.","limitations":["Some coverage and outcome figures are from official program reporting and may not be independently verified in the source.","The cases are illustrative and do not measure the full national incidence of program benefits or failures."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":16,"end_unit":18,"fact_summary":"After Hurricane Agatha, federal aid arrived in some communities and emergency assets were deployed, but ARTICLE 19 reports that authorities failed to provide clear reconstruction plans, follow-up visits, coordinated three-level governance, accessible information, and impact data; military and National Guard control of resources reduced transparency, and vulnerable Indigenous communities remained exposed.","question_ids":["2B.8","2B.10","3B.7","3B.9","3B.10","4B.6","4B.7","5B.6","5B.7","5B.9","5B.10","6B.3","6B.5","6B.6","6B.8","6B.10","8B.5","8B.6","8B.7","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The disaster occurred in 2022; the report was published in 2023 and evaluates the response relevant to the target-year posture.","ruler_attribution":"The report identifies federal, state, municipal, Sedena, and National Guard roles; it specifically links federal announcements and resource control to the response.","limitations":["Emergency response outcomes were affected by the hurricane and subnational capacity.","The source reports incomplete official information, limiting assessment of all actions taken."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":20,"end_unit":25,"fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19 documents systematic press violence and intimidation, including 696 attacks, 12 killings, state actors as the largest identified perpetrator category, criminal-group presence across much of the country, and concentrated official advertising spending: ten media companies received 54.8% of federal communication spending. It states that official discourse and discretionary advertising can function as indirect censorship.","question_ids":["2B.6","2B.8","2B.10","3B.3","3B.6","3B.8","3B.10","4B.3","4B.6","4B.9","4B.10","5B.5","7B.9","7B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The quantitative data concern 2022 and describe conditions inherited by 2023.","ruler_attribution":"Advertising figures concern the federal government; other perpetrator data include state, criminal, private, and unidentified actors.","limitations":["The source does not prove that every concentrated advertising allocation was personally ordered by López Obrador.","Criminal-group control and violence impose external constraints on federal policy."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":27,"end_unit":28,"fact_summary":"Journalist Lourdes Maldonado publicly sought presidential protection in 2019 after threats linked to her dispute with a politically powerful former governor; she was later killed in 2022 despite protection measures. Three material perpetrators were convicted through an abbreviated process, but the alleged intellectual authorship and motive were not fully investigated, according to ARTICLE 19.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.8","3B.9","3B.10","4B.3","4B.10","7B.2","7B.7","8B.8","8B.9"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The request for protection and killing occurred before 2023; the convictions and unresolved investigation define the target-year accountability posture.","ruler_attribution":"López Obrador personally received the request and referred her to federal communication officials; protection and investigation involved federal and Baja California authorities.","limitations":["The report does not establish presidential responsibility for the killing.","The abbreviated convictions are a judicial outcome, while ARTICLE 19 disputes their completeness."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":32,"end_unit":34,"fact_summary":"In 2022 ARTICLE 19 recorded 32 judicial or administrative harassment proceedings against journalists, with Yucatán accounting for nine; journalists reported intimidation, high legal costs, reputational harm, and self-censorship. The state-level defamation offense remained in force despite a commitment to repeal it, and gender-violence provisions were reportedly used in some cases involving reporting on corruption or nepotism.","question_ids":["3B.3","3B.8","3B.10","4B.3","4B.6","4B.7","4B.9","4B.10","7B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"Evidence concerns 2022 and informs the legal and civic environment entering 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The proceedings were primarily state-level; the report also evaluates the broader federal and electoral legal environment.","limitations":["The report does not attribute the individual Yucatán proceedings to López Obrador.","The gender-violence legal framework can protect women but may be applied restrictively, according to the source."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":36,"end_unit":36,"fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19 states that Mexico's federal protection, prosecution, and victim institutions possess formal legal tools but have not prevented systematic press violence; it reports that the president continued stigmatizing discourse in January 2023 and that officials' promises to end impunity had not translated into effective prevention, justice, or repair.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.3","3B.4","3B.8","3B.10","4B.3","4B.6","4B.10","7B.1","7B.2","7B.10","8B.6","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The unit includes a January 2023 presidential statement and summarizes the preceding four years, directly fitting the target year.","ruler_attribution":"The report directly attributes the January 2023 statement to López Obrador and evaluates federal institutions under his administration.","limitations":["The source is an advocacy assessment and does not provide a full government response record.","The statement that reforms were ineffective is evaluative rather than a single adjudicated finding."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":38,"end_unit":40,"fact_summary":"The administration expanded military authority: the National Guard's operational and administrative command was transferred to the Army, military domestic-security deployment was extended to 2028, and ARTICLE 19 reports that this occurred despite prior grave-rights-violation judgments and concerns about military impunity and surveillance.","question_ids":["2B.2","2B.4","2B.8","2B.10","3B.2","3B.4","3B.5","3B.6","3B.9","3B.10","4B.4","4B.5","4B.10","8B.2","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The statutory and executive decisions occurred in 2022 and establish the institutional posture entering 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes the reforms and extension to federal executive and legislative action under López Obrador.","limitations":["The source emphasizes risks and prior violations rather than measuring all security outcomes.","The National Guard's constitutional status and practical command arrangements are contested in the source's discussion."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":41,"end_unit":45,"fact_summary":"The 2022 Guacamaya disclosures and related investigations reported military surveillance of journalists, activists, and defenders, including Pegasus cases; ARTICLE 19 states that the president denied the evidence and official sites funded a campaign to contest it, while Sedena denied or withheld contracting information and legislators pursued restrictive cybersecurity proposals rather than transparent surveillance safeguards.","question_ids":["1B.3","1B.7","1B.9","1B.10","3B.2","3B.4","3B.5","3B.8","4B.3","4B.6","4B.9","4B.10","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","7B.10","8B.8","8B.9"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The disclosures, official responses, and legislative activity occurred in 2022 and remained unresolved at the start of 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes the military surveillance and official responses to federal institutions under López Obrador, while noting legislative involvement across parties.","limitations":["The source does not report a final judicial determination for every disclosed surveillance incident.","Some claims rely on leaked documents and civil-society investigations."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":47,"end_unit":48,"fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19 reports weakened rule-of-law and victim institutions, including a vacant or underfunded federal victim commission, only one National Victim System session in almost ten years, large military-civil budget disparities, and government rhetoric that frames victims as seeking benefits; it also records an official meeting and announced plan to strengthen victim attention.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.4","3B.10","4B.4","4B.10","6B.1","6B.2","6B.4","6B.5","6B.9","6B.10","7B.10","8B.2","8B.3","8B.5","8B.6","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The evidence concerns 2022-early 2023 institutional conditions.","ruler_attribution":"The report evaluates federal institutions and budgets under López Obrador and identifies an official federal commitment to strengthen victim services.","limitations":["Some figures concern Mexico City institutions rather than federal government alone.","The announced reinstatement or strengthening of coordination had not yet demonstrated outcomes in the cited units."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":61,"end_unit":63,"fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19 reports that many high-level institutional appointments remained pending: only five of 25 vacancies were filled in the described period, leaving bodies such as Cofece, IFT, Inai, and others impaired or at risk of lacking quorum; the Supreme Court ordered the Executive to submit pending Cofece proposals.","question_ids":["4B.4","4B.5","4B.10","5B.2","5B.5","5B.7","5B.10","6B.4","6B.9","7B.5","7B.6","8B.4","8B.5","8B.6","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The appointment backlog existed at the end of 2022 and continued into early 2023, directly relevant to the target year.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes omissions to both the Executive and Senate, with the Supreme Court specifically finding an Executive duty regarding Cofece proposals.","limitations":["The source's vacancy total aggregates offices with different appointing authorities.","It does not assess the qualifications of every appointment that was made."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":66,"end_unit":68,"fact_summary":"For Ayotzinapa, the GIEI reported prior military and police knowledge, intelligence monitoring, unauthorized interception, and omitted military reports; the federal government called the disappearance a state crime and sought arrests, but evidence used in its account was later questioned, arrests were cancelled or disrupted, and the special prosecutor resigned amid allegations of political interference.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.10","4B.3","4B.4","4B.10","7B.1","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The evidence is from 2022 and directly describes the accountability posture entering 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes the state-crime designation, presidential intervention in document access, and federal prosecutorial actions to the López Obrador administration.","limitations":["The underlying disappearance occurred in 2014, before López Obrador's presidency.","The report presents competing official, expert, family, and civil-society accounts; final responsibility remained unresolved in the cited units."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":71,"end_unit":72,"fact_summary":"The government acknowledged a disappearance and forensic crisis, but ARTICLE 19 reports that the National Forensic Data Bank and related registry were not operational as legally required, the disappearance registry lacked transparent methodology and open data, and the FGR resisted a court order to create the forensic bank; families consequently had to pursue searches and legal remedies.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.4","3B.6","3B.7","3B.10","4B.6","4B.10","6B.5","6B.6","6B.10","7B.2","7B.7","8B.2","8B.5","8B.6","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The cited legal nonimplementation and court proceedings occurred through late 2022 and early 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes the legal commitments and federal nonimplementation to the administration and identifies the FGR as the institution resisting immediate compliance.","limitations":["The disappearance crisis substantially predates the target year and has multiple causes.","A court order and government acknowledgment are positive institutional signals, but implementation was unresolved in the source."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":73,"end_unit":75,"fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19 reports that at least seven searchers were killed in 2022, 226 searchers suffered attacks from 2012-2022 according to the protection mechanism, and families continued searching because state institutions failed to provide safety, coordinated data, and effective investigations; it also reports incomplete transfer of historical military archives despite a 2019 presidential order.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.7","3B.9","3B.10","4B.4","4B.6","4B.10","6B.6","6B.10","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","7B.10","8B.5","8B.6","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The killings and archive-transfer status concern 2022 and early 2023, directly relevant to the target-year inherited posture.","ruler_attribution":"The presidential archive-transfer order and federal protection obligations are attributed to the López Obrador administration; many attacks and failures involve state and criminal actors.","limitations":["The historical violations and many attacks predate the target year and presidency.","The source reports that some federal actions existed but were incomplete or insufficient."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":76,"end_unit":77,"fact_summary":"The administration created the CoVEH and MEIF and initiated some archival and forensic work, with family participation and technical units as positive developments; however, ARTICLE 19 reports short mandates, inadequate resources, poor inter-institutional articulation, minimal identifications, weak legal enforceability, and limited military archive access.","question_ids":["3B.4","3B.10","4B.4","4B.10","6B.5","6B.9","6B.10","7B.6","7B.7","7B.10","8B.2","8B.3","8B.4","8B.5","8B.6","8B.7","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The mechanisms and their 2022 operating experience define the posture entering 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes creation of the mechanisms to presidential and federal decisions under López Obrador.","limitations":["These mechanisms address historical violations and the forensic crisis, much of which predates the target year.","The source provides qualitative assessments and selected outputs rather than a complete performance audit."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":78,"end_unit":80,"fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19's proposed freedom-of-expression agenda identifies needed reforms to constrain discretionary official advertising, repeal criminal speech restrictions, improve journalist protection, coordinate institutions, and stop official stigmatization; the agenda itself documents that these reforms remained outstanding at publication.","question_ids":["3B.3","3B.8","4B.3","4B.6","4B.9","4B.10","7B.10","8B.1","8B.2","8B.6","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"context","period_fit":"The agenda was published in the 2023 report and reflects unresolved policy gaps entering or during 2023.","ruler_attribution":"Recommendations target the Executive, Congress, federal agencies, and state authorities; they are not evidence that López Obrador adopted them.","limitations":["This is a policy agenda and does not itself establish implementation or outcomes.","The facts are about identified gaps and proposed remedies, not a score."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":81,"end_unit":85,"fact_summary":"The agenda calls for transparent appointment and accountability processes, judicial control over surveillance, transparent Pegasus-related contracting, independent investigations, anti-impunity measures, protection against digital censorship, and inclusive connectivity; its inclusion of these measures indicates unresolved institutional and digital-rights risks.","question_ids":["1B.3","1B.7","1B.9","3B.4","3B.8","4B.4","4B.6","4B.9","4B.10","6B.2","6B.3","6B.8","6B.10","7B.6","7B.7","8B.2","8B.5","8B.6","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"context","period_fit":"The agenda appears in a 2023 publication and summarizes unresolved conditions relevant to 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The recommendations address federal executive, legislative, judicial, prosecutorial, regulatory, and military institutions; they do not prove personal adoption or rejection by López Obrador.","limitations":["This is a reform agenda, not an independent measurement of completed policy.","It should not be treated as evidence that every proposed safeguard was absent in practice."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":87,"end_unit":89,"fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19 recommends culturally accessible proactive information, disaster-prevention planning, transparent appointments, independent information institutions, and accountability for protest-related abuses, while stating that Indigenous and vulnerable communities lacked adequate information and participation and that official institutions remained insufficiently coordinated.","question_ids":["3B.7","3B.8","3B.9","4B.4","4B.6","4B.7","4B.10","5B.7","6B.2","6B.3","6B.5","6B.6","6B.8","6B.10","8B.2","8B.5","8B.6","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"context","period_fit":"The recommendations and reported gaps are published in 2023 and concern the target-year institutional environment.","ruler_attribution":"The agenda assigns responsibilities across federal, state, and local authorities; it does not establish that López Obrador personally accepted or implemented the measures.","limitations":["This unit primarily contains proposed remedies and normative standards.","The source's conclusions about institutional insufficiency are advocacy findings, not a complete government self-assessment."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a5b157ea97d69d8","start_unit":91,"end_unit":95,"fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19 describes a documented methodology using interviews, multiple-source corroboration, official information requests, monitoring of presidential discourse, administrative records, and government and academic reports; the report primarily covers 2022 while using earlier evidence for comparison.","question_ids":["7B.1","7B.7","8B.1","8B.7"],"polarity":"context","period_fit":"This unit establishes the source's coverage and evidentiary method for the 2023 publication.","ruler_attribution":"The methodology concerns the report's evaluation of federal and subnational authorities, including López Obrador's administration.","limitations":["Methodological description is not itself a substantive fact about the ruler's conduct.","The report combines current-period evidence with historical comparisons and earlier documentation."]}],"documents_with_no_material_fact":[],"batch_limitations":["The supplied document is an ARTICLE 19 annual report focused mainly on 2022, published in 2023; it provides substantial evidence for the 2023 starting posture but limited full-year 2023 outcome evidence.","The source is an advocacy and human-rights report combining official statistics, legal records, interviews, prior reports, and evaluative judgments; attribution to López Obrador is stronger for presidential statements, federal decisions, and federal institutions than for state, municipal, criminal, or private conduct.","No evidence in the supplied document materially addresses nuclear weapons, arms control, proliferation, or other existential-risk governance beyond general cyber and surveillance concerns; therefore no separate nuclear-risk facts are asserted."]}
